claims.text: Rapid energy input enables successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles by kinetically trapping nascent particles.
Rapid energy input suppresses nanoparticle coalescence.
Atomic diffusion associated with coalescence leads to surface segregation.
The relevant starting material is a near-equimolar noble metal–containing nanoparticle system that includes Au and Cu.
The starting nanoparticles are metastable and have not yet undergone significant atomic diffusion.
Changing the rate of energy input controls the rate or occurrence of nanoparticle coalescence.
Differential elemental surface energies drive surface segregation during coalescence.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than the other constituent elements and therefore preferentially segregate to nanoparticle surfaces.
Slower energy input permits more coalescence, increases local diffusion, and promotes elemental segregation.
Rapid energy input will produce nanoparticles with a more homogeneous alloy composition and less surface segregation than slower energy input.
A slower-energy-input condition will exhibit pronounced accumulation of Au, Cu, or other low-surface-energy elements at nanoparticle surfaces.
The conventional energy-input baseline exhibits intermediate levels of coalescence and surface segregation.
The mechanism applies when kinetic trapping is achievable and surface diffusion remains active.
The mechanism may not apply to systems that reach full thermodynamic equilibrium.
The mechanism may not apply to alloys whose constituent elements have negligible surface-energy differences.
The energy-input threshold required to minimize coalescence and segregation is not yet known.

contradictions.description: The slower-energy-input baseline is predicted to show pronounced segregation, while the baseline field describes the conventional input-rate process as showing only intermediate segregation and coalescence. It is unclear whether these are the same baseline.
